Garran Hill
Some houses hold history. This one shaped it.
— I — Provenance
The Gate · 1916
Built in 1916.
Named by Walter Hines Page.
The iron, the brick columns, the long drive curving beyond them — these are the proportions Leonard Tufts' craftsmen passed through in 1915. The gate has been open since 1916.
Walter Hines Page · 1855–1918
He named it
Garran Hill.

Ambassador to the Court of St. James's. Friend of Britain in her sorest need. He directed the construction of this house from London, 3,500 miles away, by letter.

His son Ralph supervised on the ground. Leonard Tufts sent the craftsmen -- the same men building Pinehurst.

He never spent a night here as its owner.

“Build the farm, therefore; and let me hear at every stage of that happy game.”
WHP to Ralph Page — Life and Letters, Vol. I, p. 356
“Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn’t I?”
Aberdeen Station · December 11, 1918
Neo-Georgian · 1915–1916
The proportions
were not
accidental.

Six thousand and seventy-two square feet. Four point one-five acres. Seven fireplaces.

Neo-Georgian in form. The symmetry, the brick, the twelve-over-twelve sash windows -- all deliberate choices from a man who had spent years in English country houses as Ambassador.

He knew what he was asking for. The foreman, J.R. McQueen, knew how to build it.

1916 Year of completion
Original plans · 1915
Garran Hill · 1916 The door has been open since 1916. One hundred and nine years. The house is still here.

The Restoration · 1999–2001
What was original
stayed original.

The 1999 restoration took two years. Every original mantel stayed. The leaded glass stayed. The oak floors stayed.

The kitchen was rebuilt -- not renovated. Reclaimed heart-pine, laid new. The seven fireplaces were converted to propane, one kept original.

Not renovated into anonymity.
Restored back into itself.

The brass key plates on every door still have their original keys.

The House
The house still holds.

Six rooms. Seven mantels. One hundred and nine years of knowing who came through the door.

The rooms
The Entry Hall
The staircase has turned
the same curve since 1916.

Mahogany volute. Original oak floors. The hall runs straight through to the rear of the house -- visible from the moment the door opens. No wall has moved. You feel the proportions before you understand them.

The Salon
Two seating areas.
Room enough to dance.

Georgian panel molding in a full grid. Original oak floors lifted, repaired, relaid exactly as they were. Two seating areas anchored by a carved mantel.

The proportions came from the 1916 drawings. The room was built once and has not been rethought since.

The room the house was built around.
The Drawing Room
Fire going,
no one home yet.

The Delft tile surround -- blue and white, hand-painted, original -- is not a detail. It is the room. The coffered ceiling was enlarged for dancing. Everything else was chosen to answer it.

That is not decorating. That is a century of conviction.

The dining room holds the same silence.
The Dining Room
The shell cabinets
were already there.

The frontispiece above the fireplace is original -- carved in 1916, still in place. The arched niche, the wainscoting, the brass chandelier. The room seats twelve without crowding.

It holds the silence after dinner without trying.

The shell cabinets are original. The kitchen is not. Both are right.
The Kitchen
The only room
rebuilt from scratch.
Done correctly.

Reclaimed heart-pine floors -- the only room in the house not original oak. Built in the restoration, 1999–2001, from fresh drawings. White cabinetry. Dark granite. Center island. Two farm sinks. Butler's pantry. Sub-Zero. Wolf 60". Wall of windows over the rear grounds.

The kitchen is not original to 1916. It is original to the restoration.
The Library
The room the man who
founded Doubleday
would have claimed.

Three walls of shelving, floor to ceiling. Rolling ladder. French doors to the rear grounds. The restoration architect drew this room to the same standard as the 1916 house it joined.

When you stand in it, you cannot find the seam.

Dead center of the first floor. Positioned that way in the drawings.
The Primary Suite
A commission,
not a renovation.

Every panel, every cabinet, the fireplace surround -- drawn from scratch in 2000 to match a house built 84 years earlier. You cannot tell the difference. That was the point.

The dogwood blooms every April. The window has not moved.

The brass key plates on every door still have their original keys.
The Jewel Box
Fuchsia.
Chinoiserie.
Tennessee marble.

The powder room that stops people. Fuchsia chinoiserie wallpaper, floor to ceiling. Original mirror. Tennessee marble vanity.

Nobody expected it. That was also the point.

The house saves its most unexpected room for last.
4.15 Acres · Pinehurst
In 1916, those were saplings.
Now they are a forest.
Leonard Tufts provided the craftsmen -- the same men building Pinehurst. The saltwater pool sits southwest of the house: 20 by 40 feet. The holly trees at the front corners were here when Betty Dumaine renamed it Hollycrest.
200 Hollycrest Drive · Pinehurst, NC · $4,250,000
— VII — The Record
The Second Steward · 1959–1984
She arrived in 1959.
She renamed it.
She stayed.

Betty Dumaine bought the house in 1959 and renamed it Hollycrest. She brought horses, hounds, and peacocks. She planted the rose garden, the camellias, the magnolias, the dogwoods.

In 1919, at a finishing school in Cambridge, she had met a young Thai woman named Khun Sangwan Chukramol. They became roommates. Khun Sangwan later married Prince Mahidol of Songkla and became the Princess Mother of Thailand -- mother of two kings.

Betty ran her Thai charity operations from this house. She founded a horse-riding club, raised funds to build schools in Northern Thailand, set up operations in Pinehurst. The Thai royal family knew this address.

She died in 1984 at age 84. She left funds to the TPMCF, which still operates at tpmcf.org.

Betty Dumaine put the first flowers here. Someone still does.
